# Two thousand years at a glance {.unnumbered}

![Two thousand years of shrinking distance](/maps/output/comparison.png){#fig-comparison fig-alt="Line chart, on a log scale, of the fastest journey from Paris to seven cities from AD 200 to today: flat until 1800, falling steeply to 1975, then flat" aria-describedby="desc-comparison"}

::: {#desc-comparison}
The chart brings together the travel-time tables from every chapter, for seven destinations. Its scale is logarithmic, so each gridline marks a jump of several times: from an hour to six hours, to a day, a week, a month. Most of the values are estimates; each chapter's table says which.

Three things stand out. First, for most of history nothing happened: the lines barely move for some fifteen centuries, and several rise between Roman times and the Middle Ages; only the new roads and coaches of the late 18th century begin to pull them down. Second, the collapse came fast. Between 1800 and 1950, Bombay fell from about four months to a day and a half, London from four and a half days to three hours. Third, the lines flatten after 1975. For long journeys, today's travel times are much the same as fifty years ago, and a few, such as Moscow, which has had no direct flights from France since 2022, are slower.
:::
